packs.title: Python interview
packs.blurb: Common Python interview questions researched from public lists (GIL, data model, collections, concurrency).

questions.text: What is the difference between a list and a tuple?
hints: Tuple can be a dict key.
questions.rubric: A list is mutable; a tuple is not. Tuples are a bit smaller and faster, and a tuple of hashable items can be a dict key. Use a list when the sequence will grow or change; use a tuple for fixed records and return values. A one-element tuple needs a trailing comma: (1,).
questions.answer: A list is mutable; a tuple is not. Tuples are a bit smaller and faster, and a tuple of hashable items can be a dict key. Use a list when the sequence will grow or change; use a tuple for fixed records and return values. A one-element tuple needs a trailing comma: (1,).

questions.text: What is the difference between == and is in Python?
questions.rubric: == calls __eq__ and compares values. is compares object identity (the same object in memory). None checks should use is; interned small ints and interned strings can make is look like == and mislead you.
questions.answer: == calls __eq__ and compares values. is compares object identity (the same object in memory). None checks should use is; interned small ints and interned strings can make is look like == and mislead you.

questions.text: Why can a list not be used as a dictionary key?
questions.rubric: Dict keys must be hashable. A list is mutable, so its contents can change after it is inserted, which would break the hash table. A tuple of hashable items is fine.
questions.answer: Dict keys must be hashable. A list is mutable, so its contents can change after it is inserted, which would break the hash table. A tuple of hashable items is fine.

questions.rubric: *args collects extra positional arguments into a tuple. **kwargs collects extra keyword arguments into a dict. In a call, * unpacks a sequence and ** unpacks a mapping. Use them for wrappers and forwarders, not to hide a messy API.
questions.answer: *args collects extra positional arguments into a tuple. **kwargs collects extra keyword arguments into a dict. In a call, * unpacks a sequence and ** unpacks a mapping. Use them for wrappers and forwarders, not to hide a messy API.

questions.text: What is a Python decorator, and when does it run?
questions.rubric: A decorator is a callable that takes a function and returns a wrapped function. The @ syntax runs at import/definition time, not at call time. Use functools.wraps so __name__ and help stay on the original.
questions.answer: A decorator is a callable that takes a function and returns a wrapped function. The @ syntax runs at import/definition time, not at call time. Use functools.wraps so __name__ and help stay on the original.

questions.text: What is the late-binding closure pitfall in a loop?
hints: Loop vars all share the last value.
questions.rubric: A nested function looks up free variables at call time, not at definition. lambdas in a for-loop all see the last value of the loop variable. Bind it as a default: lambda i=i: i.
questions.answer: A nested function looks up free variables at call time, not at definition. lambdas in a for-loop all see the last value of the loop variable. Bind it as a default: lambda i=i: i.

questions.text: Why is a mutable default argument a bug?
questions.rubric: Default values are evaluated once, when the function is defined. A default list or dict is shared across calls, so appends leak between invocations. Use None and create the list inside the function.
questions.answer: Default values are evaluated once, when the function is defined. A default list or dict is shared across calls, so appends leak between invocations. Use None and create the list inside the function.

questions.text: What is the difference between a shallow copy and a deep copy?
questions.rubric: copy.copy / slicing copies the outer container only; nested objects are shared. copy.deepcopy walks the graph and clones nested objects. Shallow is enough for a list of ints; nested dicts of lists need deep copy.
questions.answer: copy.copy / slicing copies the outer container only; nested objects are shared. copy.deepcopy walks the graph and clones nested objects. Shallow is enough for a list of ints; nested dicts of lists need deep copy.

questions.rubric: Name lookup order is Local, Enclosing, Global, Built-in. Assignment without global/nonlocal creates a local. Use global to write a module name, nonlocal to write an enclosing function's name.
questions.answer: Name lookup order is Local, Enclosing, Global, Built-in. Assignment without global/nonlocal creates a local. Use global to write a module name, nonlocal to write an enclosing function's name.

questions.text: What is the difference between __new__ and __init__?
questions.rubric: __new__ is a static constructor that allocates and returns the instance (or another object). __init__ initializes that instance. Immutable types and metaclasses customize __new__; day-to-day classes use __init__.
questions.answer: __new__ is a static constructor that allocates and returns the instance (or another object). __init__ initializes that instance. Immutable types and metaclasses customize __new__; day-to-day classes use __init__.

questions.text: What is the method resolution order (MRO)?
questions.rubric: MRO is the linear order Python uses to find attributes on a class, C3 linearization. See Class.__mro__ or Class.mro(). super() follows that order, which is how cooperative multiple inheritance works.
questions.answer: MRO is the linear order Python uses to find attributes on a class, C3 linearization. See Class.__mro__ or Class.mro(). super() follows that order, which is how cooperative multiple inheritance works.

questions.text: How does super() work in Python 3?
questions.rubric: super() returns a proxy that continues the MRO after the current class. In a cooperative diamond, every override should call super() so each class runs once. Do not hard-code the parent class name.
questions.answer: super() returns a proxy that continues the MRO after the current class. In a cooperative diamond, every override should call super() so each class runs once. Do not hard-code the parent class name.

questions.rubric: An object with __enter__ and __exit__. with calls enter, then exit in a finally — even on exception. Use it for locks, files, and sessions so cleanup cannot be skipped.
questions.answer: An object with __enter__ and __exit__. with calls enter, then exit in a finally — even on exception. Use it for locks, files, and sessions so cleanup cannot be skipped.

questions.text: What is the difference between @classmethod and @staticmethod?
questions.rubric: @classmethod receives the class as cls — use it for alternate constructors. @staticmethod is a namespaced function with no cls/self. Prefer classmethod when you need the actual subclass.
questions.answer: @classmethod receives the class as cls — use it for alternate constructors. @staticmethod is a namespaced function with no cls/self. Prefer classmethod when you need the actual subclass.

questions.rubric: It turns a method into an attribute: obj.x calls the getter. Pair with .setter to validate writes. It is a descriptor, so it works on the class, not a per-instance function.
questions.answer: It turns a method into an attribute: obj.x calls the getter. Pair with .setter to validate writes. It is a descriptor, so it works on the class, not a per-instance function.

questions.rubric: __slots__ lists allowed attribute names and skips the per-instance __dict__. That saves memory on many small objects. You cannot assign undeclared attributes unless you also include '__dict__'.
questions.answer: __slots__ lists allowed attribute names and skips the per-instance __dict__. That saves memory on many small objects. You cannot assign undeclared attributes unless you also include '__dict__'.

hints: Data descriptors win over the instance dict.
questions.rubric: An object with __get__/__set__/__delete__ stored on the class. Functions, properties, and classmethods are descriptors. Data descriptors (with __set__) override instance dict entries.
questions.answer: An object with __get__/__set__/__delete__ stored on the class. Functions, properties, and classmethods are descriptors. Data descriptors (with __set__) override instance dict entries.

questions.rubric: The class of a class. type is the default. A metaclass's __new__/__init__ run when the class body finishes — for ORMs, ABCs, and registries. Most code should not write one.
questions.answer: The class of a class. type is the default. A metaclass's __new__/__init__ run when the class body finishes — for ORMs, ABCs, and registries. Most code should not write one.

questions.rubric: EAFP: try the operation, catch the exception (Pythonic). LBYL: check first (if key in d). EAFP avoids races between check and use; LBYL is clearer when the miss is common and cheap.
questions.answer: EAFP: try the operation, catch the exception (Pythonic). LBYL: check first (if key in d). EAFP avoids races between check and use; LBYL is clearer when the miss is common and cheap.

questions.rubric: If it quacks like a duck, it is a duck: you care about methods, not a nominal type. File-like objects and iterators work this way. Protocols/ABCs document the shape when you need a name.
questions.answer: If it quacks like a duck, it is a duck: you care about methods, not a nominal type. File-like objects and iterators work this way. Protocols/ABCs document the shape when you need a name.

questions.text: What is the difference between a module and a package?
questions.rubric: A module is a .py file (or C extension). A package is a directory with __init__.py (or a namespace package without it). import pkg.mod loads the package then the module.
questions.answer: A module is a .py file (or C extension). A package is a directory with __init__.py (or a namespace package without it). import pkg.mod loads the package then the module.

questions.rubric: __name__ is "__main__" only when the file is the entry script. Importing the file as a module does not run that block. Put CLI and demo code there so imports stay side-effect light.
questions.answer: __name__ is "__main__" only when the file is the entry script. Importing the file as a module does not run that block. Put CLI and demo code there so imports stay side-effect light.

questions.rubric: It isolates project dependencies from the system Python and from other projects. pip install then cannot break OS tools. Recreate it from requirements.txt or a lockfile.
questions.answer: It isolates project dependencies from the system Python and from other projects. pip install then cannot break OS tools. Recreate it from requirements.txt or a lockfile.

questions.text: What is the difference between bytes and str?
questions.rubric: str is Unicode text. bytes is raw 8-bit data. Decode bytes to str with an encoding (utf-8); encode the other way. Mixing them is a TypeError in Python 3.
questions.answer: str is Unicode text. bytes is raw 8-bit data. Decode bytes to str with an encoding (utf-8); encode the other way. Mixing them is a TypeError in Python 3.

questions.text: How does garbage collection work in CPython?
questions.rubric: CPython uses reference counting plus a cyclic GC. When a refcount hits zero the object is freed immediately. Cycles (A points at B points at A) need the generational collector.
questions.answer: CPython uses reference counting plus a cyclic GC. When a refcount hits zero the object is freed immediately. Cycles (A points at B points at A) need the generational collector.

questions.rubric: Each object tracks how many pointers refer to it. Names, containers, and call stacks all increment it. del or leaving scope decrements. sys.getrefcount is one higher because the argument itself is a ref.
questions.answer: Each object tracks how many pointers refer to it. Names, containers, and call stacks all increment it. del or leaving scope decrements. sys.getrefcount is one higher because the argument itself is a ref.

questions.text: Does Python pass by value or by reference?
questions.rubric: Neither slogan is right: it passes object references by assignment. Rebinding a parameter does not rebind the caller's name. Mutating a mutable object in place is visible to the caller.
questions.answer: Neither slogan is right: it passes object references by assignment. Rebinding a parameter does not rebind the caller's name. Mutating a mutable object in place is visible to the caller.

questions.text: What is the difference between list.append and list.extend?
questions.rubric: append adds one object as a single element (even if it is a list). extend iterates its argument and adds each item. += on a list is extend.
questions.answer: append adds one object as a single element (even if it is a list). extend iterates its argument and adds each item. += on a list is extend.

questions.text: When do you use a set?
questions.rubric: For unique membership tests in average O(1). Items must be hashable. Use for dedup, difference, and intersection. Order is insertion order in modern CPython but do not rely on it for API contracts unless you mean that.
questions.answer: For unique membership tests in average O(1). Items must be hashable. Use for dedup, difference, and intersection. Order is insertion order in modern CPython but do not rely on it for API contracts unless you mean that.

questions.rubric: An immutable set. It is hashable, so it can be a dict key or a member of another set. Use it when a set of tags must itself be a key.
questions.answer: An immutable set. It is hashable, so it can be a dict key or a member of another set. Use it when a set of tags must itself be a key.

hints: Lazy, one value at a time.
questions.rubric: (x*x for x in xs) is lazy: it yields one value at a time. sum(x*x for x in xs) never builds the list. Parentheses, not square brackets — square brackets are a list comprehension and allocate everything.
questions.answer: (x*x for x in xs) is lazy: it yields one value at a time. sum(x*x for x in xs) never builds the list. Parentheses, not square brackets — square brackets are a list comprehension and allocate everything.

questions.rubric: It delegates to a subgenerator: yields its values, forwards .send/.throw, and returns the subgenerator's StopIteration value. It flattens nested generators without a manual loop.
questions.answer: It delegates to a subgenerator: yields its values, forwards .send/.throw, and returns the subgenerator's StopIteration value. It flattens nested generators without a manual loop.

questions.rubric: An iterable's __iter__ returns an iterator. An iterator has __iter__ (returns self) and __next__, which raises StopIteration when done. for x in xs calls iter then next until StopIteration.
questions.answer: An iterable's __iter__ returns an iterator. An iterator has __iter__ (returns self) and __next__, which raises StopIteration when done. for x in xs calls iter then next until StopIteration.

questions.text: What does else on a for loop mean?
questions.rubric: The else runs if the loop did not break. Use it for "search failed" after a for with a break on success. It is not "run when empty."
questions.answer: The else runs if the loop did not break. Use it for "search failed" after a for with a break on success. It is not "run when empty."

questions.text: What does else on try mean?
hints: Keep success-path exceptions out of except.
questions.rubric: else runs when no exception was raised in try. Use it for code that should not catch exceptions from the success path. finally still runs after else.
questions.answer: else runs when no exception was raised in try. Use it for code that should not catch exceptions from the success path. finally still runs after else.

questions.rubric: Yes for normal exceptions, return, and break — with a catch: os._exit, a crash, or a kill -9 skip it. Do not use finally for locks if you also return inside try without care; the with statement is clearer.
questions.answer: Yes for normal exceptions, return, and break — with a catch: os._exit, a crash, or a kill -9 skip it. Do not use finally for locks if you also return inside try without care; the with statement is clearer.

questions.text: What is the difference between Exception and BaseException?
questions.rubric: Exception is the user-catchable hierarchy. BaseException also includes SystemExit, KeyboardInterrupt, and GeneratorExit. except Exception does not swallow Ctrl-C; except: or except BaseException does.
questions.answer: Exception is the user-catchable hierarchy. BaseException also includes SystemExit, KeyboardInterrupt, and GeneratorExit. except Exception does not swallow Ctrl-C; except: or except BaseException does.

questions.rubric: A memoizing decorator with a max size and LRU eviction. Arguments must be hashable. Use cache_info() in tests. For unbound growth use cache; for identity by id it is the wrong tool.
questions.answer: A memoizing decorator with a max size and LRU eviction. Arguments must be hashable. Use cache_info() in tests. For unbound growth use cache; for identity by id it is the wrong tool.

questions.text: Why does a decorator need functools.wraps?
questions.rubric: Without wraps, the wrapper's __name__, __doc__, and signature hide the original. wraps copies those attributes so help(), logging, and tests still see the wrapped function.
questions.answer: Without wraps, the wrapper's __name__, __doc__, and signature hide the original. wraps copies those attributes so help(), logging, and tests still see the wrapped function.

questions.rubric: It freezes some arguments of a callable and returns a new callable. Use it instead of a lambda when you only want to bind args. The original function is on .func.
questions.answer: It freezes some arguments of a callable and returns a new callable. Use it instead of a lambda when you only want to bind args. The original function is on .func.

questions.text: When do you use a dataclass versus a namedtuple?
questions.rubric: namedtuple is an immutable tuple with names — cheap, unpackable, hashable. dataclass is a generated class: optional frozen, defaults, and methods. Prefer dataclass unless you need tuple unpacking or a tiny record.
questions.answer: namedtuple is an immutable tuple with names — cheap, unpackable, hashable. dataclass is a generated class: optional frozen, defaults, and methods. Prefer dataclass unless you need tuple unpacking or a tiny record.

questions.rubric: If a == b then hash(a) must equal hash(b), or dict/set lookup breaks. Mutable objects that define __eq__ should set __hash__ = None. Frozen dataclasses get both generated together.
questions.answer: If a == b then hash(a) must equal hash(b), or dict/set lookup breaks. Mutable objects that define __eq__ should set __hash__ = None. Frozen dataclasses get both generated together.

questions.rubric: A dict of counts. most_common(n), subtract, and + combine histograms. Handy for frequencies and bag-of-words. Values can go negative after subtract.
questions.answer: A dict of counts. most_common(n), subtract, and + combine histograms. Handy for frequencies and bag-of-words. Values can go negative after subtract.

hints: Not when missing is a bug.
questions.rubric: A dict that calls a factory for missing keys (list, int, set). d[k].append(x) never KeyErrors. Do not use it when missing should be an error — that hides bugs.
questions.answer: A dict that calls a factory for missing keys (list, int, set). d[k].append(x) never KeyErrors. Do not use it when missing should be an error — that hides bugs.

questions.text: When is a deque better than a list?
questions.rubric: O(1) appends and pops on both ends. A list is O(n) at the left. Use deque for queues and sliding windows. It is not for random indexing of a huge buffer.
questions.answer: O(1) appends and pops on both ends. A list is O(n) at the left. Use deque for queues and sliding windows. It is not for random indexing of a huge buffer.

questions.rubric: A binary heap in a plain list. heappush/heappop give a min-heap. Use nsmallest/nlargest for top-k. There is no max-heap type — negate numbers or wrap in tuples.
questions.answer: A binary heap in a plain list. heappush/heappop give a min-heap. Use nsmallest/nlargest for top-k. There is no max-heap type — negate numbers or wrap in tuples.

questions.rubric: := assigns inside an expression: while (line := f.readline()). Use it to avoid computing twice. Do not nest it into unreadable conditions.
questions.answer: := assigns inside an expression: while (line := f.readline()). Use it to avoid computing twice. Do not nest it into unreadable conditions.

questions.rubric: Structural pattern matching (3.10+). It can match literals, sequences, mappings, and class patterns. Use a discriminant field like OOP switch, and a catch-all case _.
questions.answer: Structural pattern matching (3.10+). It can match literals, sequences, mappings, and class patterns. Use a discriminant field like OOP switch, and a catch-all case _.

questions.text: What is the difference between __str__ and __repr__?
questions.rubric: __str__ is for users (print). __repr__ is for developers (debug, the REPL) and should be unambiguous, ideally round-trippable. If you only define one, define __repr__.
questions.answer: __str__ is for users (print). __repr__ is for developers (debug, the REPL) and should be unambiguous, ideally round-trippable. If you only define one, define __repr__.

questions.rubric: Attributes starting with __ but not ending with __ are renamed to _ClassName__attr. It is not true privacy — it avoids subclass clashes. Use a single underscore for "internal".
questions.answer: Attributes starting with __ but not ending with __ are renamed to _ClassName__attr. It is not true privacy — it avoids subclass clashes. Use a single underscore for "internal".

questions.rubric: An abstract base class (abc.ABC) that can declare @abstractmethod. Instantiating a subclass that skipped those methods fails. Use ABCs for virtual subclasses and isinstance checks.
questions.answer: An abstract base class (abc.ABC) that can declare @abstractmethod. Instantiating a subclass that skipped those methods fails. Use ABCs for virtual subclasses and isinstance checks.

questions.text: What is typing.Protocol versus an ABC?
questions.rubric: Protocol is structural: if the methods exist, the type matches (optionally @runtime_checkable). ABC is nominal: you inherit or register. Prefer Protocol for duck-typed libraries.
questions.answer: Protocol is structural: if the methods exist, the type matches (optionally @runtime_checkable). ABC is nominal: you inherit or register. Prefer Protocol for duck-typed libraries.

questions.rubric: Stacked @overload signatures document different call shapes; the implementation is a single function. They exist only for the type checker — at runtime only the implementation remains.
questions.answer: Stacked @overload signatures document different call shapes; the implementation is a single function. They exist only for the type checker — at runtime only the implementation remains.

questions.text: How do you break a circular import?
questions.rubric: Move the shared type to a third module, import inside the function that needs it, or use TYPE_CHECKING for type-only imports. Cycles are a design smell — flatten the graph.
questions.answer: Move the shared type to a third module, import inside the function that needs it, or use TYPE_CHECKING for type-only imports. Cycles are a design smell — flatten the graph.

questions.rubric: A list of public names for from module import *. It does not enforce privacy. Use it to keep * imports from leaking internals; explicit imports are still better.
questions.answer: A list of public names for from module import *. It does not enforce privacy. Use it to keep * imports from leaking internals; explicit imports are still better.

questions.text: When do you use pickle versus json?
questions.rubric: json is text, interoperable, and safe for untrusted data if you do not use a custom decoder that executes code. pickle serializes arbitrary Python objects and can run code on load — never unpickle untrusted bytes.
questions.answer: json is text, interoperable, and safe for untrusted data if you do not use a custom decoder that executes code. pickle serializes arbitrary Python objects and can run code on load — never unpickle untrusted bytes.

questions.rubric: eval runs any Python expression — a security hole. ast.literal_eval only accepts literals (dicts, lists, numbers, strings). Use it for slightly richer config than json.
questions.answer: eval runs any Python expression — a security hole. ast.literal_eval only accepts literals (dicts, lists, numbers, strings). Use it for slightly richer config than json.

questions.text: What changed about the GIL in Python 3.13?
questions.rubric: 3.13 ships an experimental free-threaded (no-GIL) build per PEP 703. Default CPython still has the GIL. Mention it, then say you still write I/O threads vs multiprocessing for CPU on today's default build.
questions.answer: 3.13 ships an experimental free-threaded (no-GIL) build per PEP 703. Default CPython still has the GIL. Mention it, then say you still write I/O threads vs multiprocessing for CPU on today's default build.

questions.text: When do you choose threading, multiprocessing, or asyncio?
questions.rubric: I/O-bound many waits: asyncio or threads (GIL released on I/O). CPU-bound Python: multiprocessing or a native library. Mixing: run blocking work in a thread pool from asyncio (to_thread).
questions.answer: I/O-bound many waits: asyncio or threads (GIL released on I/O). CPU-bound Python: multiprocessing or a native library. Mixing: run blocking work in a thread pool from asyncio (to_thread).

questions.rubric: A high-level pool API: ThreadPoolExecutor and ProcessPoolExecutor with submit/map. Prefer it over raw Thread/Process when you just need N workers and futures.
questions.answer: A high-level pool API: ThreadPoolExecutor and ProcessPoolExecutor with submit/map. Prefer it over raw Thread/Process when you just need N workers and futures.

questions.rubric: Two or more waiters each hold a lock the other needs. Avoid by lock ordering, using a timeout, or not holding two locks. RLock does not fix a lock-order deadlock between two objects.
questions.answer: Two or more waiters each hold a lock the other needs. Avoid by lock ordering, using a timeout, or not holding two locks. RLock does not fix a lock-order deadlock between two objects.

questions.text: What is the difference between Lock and RLock?
questions.rubric: Lock cannot be acquired twice by the same thread — that deadlocks yourself. RLock is reentrant: the owner can acquire again. Use RLock for callbacks into code that already holds the lock.
questions.answer: Lock cannot be acquired twice by the same thread — that deadlocks yourself. RLock is reentrant: the owner can acquire again. Use RLock for callbacks into code that already holds the lock.

questions.text: Why is time.sleep a bug inside asyncio?
questions.rubric: time.sleep blocks the entire event loop, so every task stalls. Use await asyncio.sleep. Same class of bug as requests.get in async def — use httpx/aiohttp.
questions.answer: time.sleep blocks the entire event loop, so every task stalls. Use await asyncio.sleep. Same class of bug as requests.get in async def — use httpx/aiohttp.

questions.text: What is the difference between asyncio.gather and create_task?
questions.rubric: create_task schedules one coroutine. gather waits on many and collects results (or raises). Tasks start when created; gather also starts them. Use TaskGroup (3.11+) for structured shutdown.
questions.answer: create_task schedules one coroutine. gather waits on many and collects results (or raises). Tasks start when created; gather also starts them. Use TaskGroup (3.11+) for structured shutdown.

questions.rubric: It makes instances callable: obj() runs obj.__call__. Use it for function-like objects that hold state (a tokenizer, a metric). Classes are already callable via type.__call__.
questions.answer: It makes instances callable: obj() runs obj.__call__. Use it for function-like objects that hold state (a tokenizer, a metric). Classes are already callable via type.__call__.

questions.rubric: It implements obj[key] — sequences, mappings, and numpy-style slices. Pair with __len__ and __iter__ for a complete container. Missing keys should raise IndexError or KeyError, not return None.
questions.answer: It implements obj[key] — sequences, mappings, and numpy-style slices. Pair with __len__ and __iter__ for a complete container. Missing keys should raise IndexError or KeyError, not return None.

questions.rubric: A zero-copy window onto bytes-like data. You can slice without copying. Use it when parsing binary buffers so you do not allocate a new bytes for every field.
questions.answer: A zero-copy window onto bytes-like data. You can slice without copying. Use it when parsing binary buffers so you do not allocate a new bytes for every field.

questions.text: When do you use pathlib instead of os.path?
questions.rubric: Path objects compose with / , have .read_text(), .glob(), and .exists(). os.path is stringly. New code should use pathlib unless an API demands strings.
questions.answer: Path objects compose with / , have .read_text(), .glob(), and .exists(). os.path is stringly. New code should use pathlib unless an API demands strings.

questions.rubric: subprocess can avoid the shell (shell=False), capture stdout/stderr, and raise on non-zero (check=True). os.system is a shell string — injection risk and no capture.
questions.answer: subprocess can avoid the shell (shell=False), capture stdout/stderr, and raise on non-zero (check=True). os.system is a shell string — injection risk and no capture.

questions.text: Why use logging instead of print?
questions.rubric: Levels, loggers per module, handlers (file, stderr), and runtime config. print cannot be filtered in production. Logger names follow the package tree.
questions.answer: Levels, loggers per module, handlers (file, stderr), and runtime config. print cannot be filtered in production. Logger names follow the package tree.

questions.text: Does NumPy care about the GIL?
hints: C loops can release the GIL.
questions.rubric: Many NumPy (and pandas) C loops release the GIL, so threads can parallelize that C work. Pure Python loops around NumPy still serialize. Profile before you add processes.
questions.answer: Many NumPy (and pandas) C loops release the GIL, so threads can parallelize that C work. Pure Python loops around NumPy still serialize. Profile before you add processes.

questions.text: Do list comprehensions leak the loop variable?
hints: Do not use the name after.
questions.rubric: In Python 3, no — the loop name is local to the comprehension. In Python 2 it leaked. Generator expressions were always scoped. Do not rely on the loop var after the comprehension.
questions.answer: In Python 3, no — the loop name is local to the comprehension. In Python 2 it leaked. Generator expressions were always scoped. Do not rely on the loop var after the comprehension.

questions.text: How do you sort with a key function?
questions.rubric: list.sort(key=...) or sorted(..., key=...). The key is computed once per item (Decorate-Sort-Undecorate). For reverse+stable, sort twice from the last key to the first.
questions.answer: list.sort(key=...) or sorted(..., key=...). The key is computed once per item (Decorate-Sort-Undecorate). For reverse+stable, sort twice from the last key to the first.

questions.rubric: Yes, Timsort is stable: equal keys keep original order. That is why you can sort by last name then first name with two passes, least-significant first.
questions.answer: Yes, Timsort is stable: equal keys keep original order. That is why you can sort by last name then first name with two passes, least-significant first.

questions.text: What does zip do, and what happens with unequal lengths?
questions.rubric: zip pairs items until the shortest iterable ends. Use itertools.zip_longest for padding. In 3.10+, zip(..., strict=True) errors on length mismatch.
questions.answer: zip pairs items until the shortest iterable ends. Use itertools.zip_longest for padding. In 3.10+, zip(..., strict=True) errors on length mismatch.

questions.text: Why use enumerate instead of range(len)?
questions.rubric: enumerate(xs) yields (index, item) and works on any iterable, not only sequences. range(len) fails on generators and is less readable.
questions.answer: enumerate(xs) yields (index, item) and works on any iterable, not only sequences. range(len) fails on generators and is less readable.

questions.rubric: It closes the file on success and on exception. A bare f = open() leaks FDs if you return early. Text mode is the default; pass encoding="utf-8" explicitly.
questions.answer: It closes the file on success and on exception. A bare f = open() leaks FDs if you return early. Text mode is the default; pass encoding="utf-8" explicitly.

questions.text: Why compare to None with is, not ==?
questions.rubric: None is a singleton, so is is correct and faster. A custom __eq__ can make == None true for other objects. linters flag == None.
questions.answer: None is a singleton, so is is correct and faster. A custom __eq__ can make == None true for other objects. linters flag == None.

questions.text: What is considered false in Python?
hints: User objects are true by default.
questions.rubric: False, None, 0, 0.0, empty str/list/dict/set, and objects whose __bool__ or __len__ returns 0. A custom class is true by default.
questions.answer: False, None, 0, 0.0, empty str/list/dict/set, and objects whose __bool__ or __len__ returns 0. A custom class is true by default.

questions.text: How do and and or return values?
questions.rubric: They return the last evaluated operand, not a coerced bool. a or b is a if a is truthy else b. That is why x = s or "default" works.
questions.answer: They return the last evaluated operand, not a coerced bool. a or b is a if a is truthy else b. That is why x = s or "default" works.

questions.text: When do you need the global keyword?
questions.rubric: Only to assign to a module-level name inside a function. Reading a global needs no keyword. If you assign without global, Python makes a local and you get UnboundLocalError on earlier reads.
questions.answer: Only to assign to a module-level name inside a function. Reading a global needs no keyword. If you assign without global, Python makes a local and you get UnboundLocalError on earlier reads.

questions.rubric: To assign to a name in an enclosing (but not global) function. Closures that increment a counter need nonlocal count. Without it you create a local.
questions.answer: To assign to a name in an enclosing (but not global) function. Closures that increment a counter need nonlocal count. Without it you create a local.

questions.rubric: A singleton. NumPy uses it for slicing. Type stubs use it in protocols and typing. Type checkers accept ... in abstract bodies. It is not a placeholder that runtime-skips.
questions.answer: A singleton. NumPy uses it for slicing. Type stubs use it in protocols and typing. Type checkers accept ... in abstract bodies. It is not a placeholder that runtime-skips.

questions.rubric: A tuple of ints of unknown length. tuple[int] is a one-int tuple. Homogeneous variadic tuples use the ellipsis.
questions.answer: A tuple of ints of unknown length. tuple[int] is a one-int tuple. Homogeneous variadic tuples use the ellipsis.

questions.rubric: A dict with a known set of keys and value types, checked by the type checker. Runtime is still a dict. Use total=False for optional keys. Not a replacement for a dataclass when you want attributes.
questions.answer: A dict with a known set of keys and value types, checked by the type checker. Runtime is still a dict. Use total=False for optional keys. Not a replacement for a dataclass when you want attributes.

questions.rubric: A type-checker-only distinct alias: UserId = NewType("UserId", int). At runtime it is a dummy callable that returns the value. It prevents mixing UserId with raw int in typed code.
questions.answer: A type-checker-only distinct alias: UserId = NewType("UserId", int). At runtime it is a dummy callable that returns the value. It prevents mixing UserId with raw int in typed code.

questions.rubric: The type of the current class, including subclasses. fluent() -> Self means a subclass method returns that subclass, not the base. Prefer it over quoting the class name.
questions.answer: The type of the current class, including subclasses. fluent() -> Self means a subclass method returns that subclass, not the base. Prefer it over quoting the class name.

questions.rubric: It captures a callable's parameter list so a decorator can keep the wrapped signature. Concatenate adds extra args. You need it for typed decorators in 3.10+.
questions.answer: It captures a callable's parameter list so a decorator can keep the wrapped signature. Concatenate adds extra args. You need it for typed decorators in 3.10+.

questions.text: What does a type checker like mypy give you?
questions.rubric: It verifies annotations without running the code: wrong keys, None, and mismatched returns. It does not prove runtime correctness. Gradual: untyped code is Any unless you forbid it.
questions.answer: It verifies annotations without running the code: wrong keys, None, and mismatched returns. It does not prove runtime correctness. Gradual: untyped code is Any unless you forbid it.

questions.text: Why can threads still help if the GIL exists?
questions.rubric: The GIL is released around many blocking I/O calls (socket, disk, some C APIs). Threads overlap those waits. CPU-bound Python bytecode does not overlap — that is when you use processes.
questions.answer: The GIL is released around many blocking I/O calls (socket, disk, some C APIs). Threads overlap those waits. CPU-bound Python bytecode does not overlap — that is when you use processes.

questions.text: What is the multiprocessing pickle gotcha?
questions.rubric: Process pools pickle the function and arguments to the child. Lambdas, nested functions, and unpickleable objects fail. Use top-level functions and simple data, or a shared-memory array.
questions.answer: Process pools pickle the function and arguments to the child. Lambdas, nested functions, and unpickleable objects fail. Use top-level functions and simple data, or a shared-memory array.

questions.rubric: A thread-safe FIFO between producer and consumer threads. task_done/join coordinate shutdown. For processes use multiprocessing.Queue. asyncio has asyncio.Queue.
questions.answer: A thread-safe FIFO between producer and consumer threads. task_done/join coordinate shutdown. For processes use multiprocessing.Queue. asyncio has asyncio.Queue.

questions.text: Why does CPython have a GIL?
questions.rubric: It keeps reference counting simple and makes C extensions easier to write by serializing bytecode. The cost is no CPU parallelism from threads. That trade was explicit; PEP 703 is the long-term unwind.
questions.answer: It keeps reference counting simple and makes C extensions easier to write by serializing bytecode. The cost is no CPU parallelism from threads. That trade was explicit; PEP 703 is the long-term unwind.

questions.text: How do C extensions deal with the GIL?
questions.rubric: They call Py_BEGIN_ALLOW_THREADS around blocking or parallel C work, then Py_END_ALLOW_THREADS. NumPy and zlib do this. If they forget, they hold the GIL and stall other threads.
questions.answer: They call Py_BEGIN_ALLOW_THREADS around blocking or parallel C work, then Py_END_ALLOW_THREADS. NumPy and zlib do this. If they forget, they hold the GIL and stall other threads.

questions.rubric: Cached bytecode in __pycache__. Python loads it when the source mtime matches, skipping parse. It is not encryption or a speedup of the algorithm — only import time.
questions.answer: Cached bytecode in __pycache__. Python loads it when the source mtime matches, skipping parse. It is not encryption or a speedup of the algorithm — only import time.

questions.text: Can you run a program from only .pyc files?
questions.rubric: Historically yes for many modules, but it is a poor distribution method. Prefer an interpreter plus source or a freeze tool. Hash-based pyc in 3.7+ changes invalidation.
questions.answer: Historically yes for many modules, but it is a poor distribution method. Prefer an interpreter plus source or a freeze tool. Hash-based pyc in 3.7+ changes invalidation.

questions.rubric: The module body: class and def statements build objects, top-level calls run. Heavy work at import slows startup and complicates tests. Keep import graphs lazy.
questions.answer: The module body: class and def statements build objects, top-level calls run. Heavy work at import slows startup and complicates tests. Keep import graphs lazy.

questions.text: Why is from module import * discouraged?
questions.rubric: It dumps names into your namespace, hides origin, breaks linters, and can overwrite names. __all__ limits the damage but explicit imports are the rule.
questions.answer: It dumps names into your namespace, hides origin, breaks linters, and can overwrite names. __all__ limits the damage but explicit imports are the rule.

questions.rubric: from . import sibling or from ..pkg import x. It only works inside a package (not a script run as __main__ from that file). Running python -m pkg.mod is the usual fix.
questions.answer: from . import sibling or from ..pkg import x. It only works inside a package (not a script run as __main__ from that file). Running python -m pkg.mod is the usual fix.

hints: Do not hack it in prod.
questions.rubric: The list of directories import searches. It starts with the script dir, then PYTHONPATH, then site-packages. Mutating it at runtime is a last resort — fix the install.
questions.answer: The list of directories import searches. It starts with the script dir, then PYTHONPATH, then site-packages. Mutating it at runtime is a last resort — fix the install.

questions.rubric: It reverses a sequence by slicing with step -1, returning a new object. For a list it copies. For reversing in place use list.reverse().
questions.answer: It reverses a sequence by slicing with step -1, returning a new object. For a list it copies. For reversing in place use list.reverse().

questions.rubric: Yes, a shallow copy of the list. Nested objects are still shared. list(xs) and copy.copy do the same outer copy.
questions.answer: Yes, a shallow copy of the list. Nested objects are still shared. list(xs) and copy.copy do the same outer copy.

questions.rubric: An integer unique for this object during its lifetime (in CPython, often the address). After the object is gone the id can be reused. Do not persist it.
questions.answer: An integer unique for this object during its lifetime (in CPython, often the address). After the object is gone the id can be reused. Do not persist it.

questions.rubric: CPython reuses some string objects (identifiers, compile-time literals that look like names). is can then succeed for equal strings. Do not rely on it; use == for text.
questions.answer: CPython reuses some string objects (identifiers, compile-time literals that look like names). is can then succeed for equal strings. Do not rely on it; use == for text.

questions.text: What is the small integer cache?
questions.rubric: CPython interned -5..256 so those ints are singletons. is works there and fails for 257. Always use == for numbers.
questions.answer: CPython interned -5..256 so those ints are singletons. is works there and fails for 257. Always use == for numbers.

questions.rubric: closing(obj) calls obj.close() in exit — for things that are not context managers. suppress(Exception) swallows that exception. Both are small with-helpers.
questions.answer: closing(obj) calls obj.close() in exit — for things that are not context managers. suppress(Exception) swallows that exception. Both are small with-helpers.

questions.rubric: A context manager that can enter an unknown number of other context managers at runtime and unwind them. Use it when the set of files or locks is dynamic.
questions.answer: A context manager that can enter an unknown number of other context managers at runtime and unwind them. Use it when the set of files or locks is dynamic.

questions.text: When do you put weakrefs in a cache?
questions.rubric: So the cache does not keep objects alive. When the last strong ref dies, the entry can vanish (with a callback). The existing Practice question: assigning a weakref does not keep the object alive.
questions.answer: So the cache does not keep objects alive. When the last strong ref dies, the entry can vanish (with a callback). The existing Practice question: assigning a weakref does not keep the object alive.

questions.text: Your workload is I/O-bound. Why is multiprocessing usually the wrong first tool?
questions.rubric: Processes copy memory, cost IPC, and start slowly. I/O already releases the GIL, so threads or asyncio overlap waits with less overhead. Reach for processes when the bottleneck is Python CPU.
questions.answer: Processes copy memory, cost IPC, and start slowly. I/O already releases the GIL, so threads or asyncio overlap waits with less overhead. Reach for processes when the bottleneck is Python CPU.
